guideTitle: Best Immersion Blenders for Whipped Cream (2026)
metaTitle: Best Immersion Blenders for Whipped Cream 2026
metaDescription: Stick blenders with whisk heads for whipped cream compared on whisk design, low-speed control, beaker size and cleanup across six models.
expertTake: The Cuisinart CSB-179 is the top pick for whipped cream, because its chef's whisk and a variable speed sweep let you whip slowly and stop at soft peaks. The Bonsenkitchen 4-in-1 is the value pick, since twenty speeds and an egg whisk cost little. Skip the blade attachment entirely for cream, because a cutting blade turns cream to butter in seconds.
introParagraphs: Whipping cream with a stick blender depends almost entirely on the whisk head. The blade that comes on the stick will turn cream to butter, but a wire whisk on the same motor traps air and thickens the cream without cutting the fat globules apart.

That puts the whisk shape, the speed range and the bowl ahead of every other spec. A slow start, a wide wire cage and a deep, cold bowl give soft peaks in about a minute, while a fast, flimsy whisk splashes cream and over-whips it. This guide compares six sticks with whisks on exactly those points.

products.name: Cuisinart CSB-179 Smart Stick variable speed hand blender
products.description:
The CSB-179 is the stick that makes whipped cream feel controlled. It ships with a chef's whisk, and the variable speed sweep runs from low to high, so you can begin barely turning and build up as the cream thickens. That slow start keeps cream in the bowl instead of on the wall.

The 300 watt DC motor is part of the reason. A DC motor holds torque at low speed, which is exactly where whipping lives: a whisk spinning at a moderate speed draws a steady stream of air into the cream. It also runs quietly enough that you can hear the sound of the cream change as it thickens, which is the cue to stop.

Use a deep, narrow bowl that is cold, with the cream chilled, and tilt the bowl slightly so the whisk stays submerged. Stop when the cream holds a soft peak and leave stiff peaks to a hand whisk. Wash the whisk right after use, since fat clings to the wires, and a drop of dish soap in warm water clears it. It is the most reassuring whipper in the group.
products.bestFor: Cooks who want slow, controlled whipping with a proper wire whisk.
pros: Chef's whisk included in the kit
Variable speed lets you start slowly
DC motor holds torque at low speed
Quiet enough to hear the cream change
cons: 300W limits thick batters with the same whisk
Chopper adds a part you may not use

products.name: Bonsenkitchen 4-in-1 500W stick blender, 20 speeds, egg whisk
products.description:
The Bonsenkitchen offers twenty speeds and an egg whisk at a low price tier, which makes it the cheapest route to fine control over cream. The twenty steps let you pick a slow, steady pace and hold it, which is the main skill in whipping. A 500 watt motor and a turbo button are there if you want them, though you should ignore the turbo for cream.

The kit includes a 24 oz beaker and a 17 oz food processor bowl, and the beaker is the right shape for a modest amount of cream. Tall and narrow, it keeps the whisk submerged, which is more important than the motor. A bowl that is too wide lets the cream spread thin so the whisk spins in air.

Expect a little splash at the start, since the whisk is a plastic-handled attachment that needs to be fully seated. Rinse the wires straight after use, and check the whisk joint for dried cream. It does not match the Cuisinart for smoothness, but it is a very capable stick for the money.
products.bestFor: First-time buyers who want twenty speeds and a whisk at a low outlay.
pros: Egg whisk and 24 oz beaker included
cons: Turbo is a trap for cream
Whisk must be fully seated or it wobbles

products.name: Braun MultiQuick 5 350W dual speed with beaker and whisk
products.description:
The MultiQuick 5 keeps whipped cream simple. It has two speeds, a whisk and a beaker, and all three are enough for a cup of cream. The 350 watt motor is not strong, but cream does not need strength, only a whisk that turns at the right pace.

Two speeds can be an advantage. Use the low one for the whole job, and you cannot over-whip by running too fast. The beaker is a good size for a single batch, and its tall shape keeps the whisk submerged.

The trade is control. With only two speeds you cannot fine tune the pace, so you rely on your eye for soft peaks. Stop the moment the cream holds a trail from the whisk. Wash the whisk by hand, and let the beaker dry before storing it. Whipping cream makes a handy second job for a stick that you already own for soup.
products.bestFor: Cooks who own a Braun for soup and want it to whip cream too.
pros: Lowest motor rating that still works
cons: Whisk wires are lighter than a dedicated mixer's

products.name: Martha Stewart 500W stick blender with 1 litre beaker
products.description:
The Martha Stewart stick pairs a 500 watt motor with a variable speed knob and a one litre beaker. The knob lets you fine tune the pace, and the listing describes simple on and off operation with a turbo mode. A one litre beaker is the largest vessel in this guide, which means you can whip a large amount of cream in one go.

The listing calls the motor quiet, and the variable knob is a good match for whipping. Set it low, hold the whisk near the surface and raise it only as the cream thickens. The large beaker has room for the cream to expand, which is important because whipped cream roughly doubles in volume.

It does not list a dedicated whisk head in the description we have, so check that the kit you are buying includes one. Wash the beaker and the head straight away, since cream residue clings to plastic. It is a sensible option for anyone who whips larger batches for a dessert or a cake.
products.bestFor: Cooks who whip larger amounts of cream and want a one litre beaker.
pros: One litre beaker leaves room for expansion
Variable speed knob for fine control
cons: Confirm a whisk head is in the kit you buy
Plastic beaker holds onto cream fat

products.name: KOIOS 1000W 3-in-1 stick blender, 12 speeds, 304 blade
products.description:
The KOIOS is a 3-in-1 set built around a 304 stainless four-tip blade, twelve speeds and an anti-scratch guard. The whisk is one of its three heads, and twelve steps give you a good range at the low end for cream. The 1000 watt number is a headline, so treat the dial as the real control.

The benefit for cream is the slow end of the dial. Start at the first step and watch the whisk. Cream goes from liquid to soft peaks within a minute, and stopping at the right time matters more than motor power. The anti-scratch guard is mostly for the blending head, so remove it if you want the whisk to sit properly.

It costs a little more than the Bonsenkitchen and offers more speed steps than the Braun. Rinse the whisk wires with warm soapy water, since cold water leaves a greasy film. It is a reasonable choice for cooks who want the same stick to handle soup, smoothies and cream.
products.bestFor: Cooks who want an all-round stick with a whisk and a twelve-step dial.
pros: Twelve speeds with a gentle low end
cons: Headline wattage is a peak-style claim
Guard must come off for the whisk

products.name: MegaWise 3-in-1 stick blender, 12 speeds, whisk and frother
products.description:
The MegaWise states a 400 watt rated DC motor and an 800 watt peak, which makes its power easy to read. It has twelve speeds with a turbo button and a kit with a whisk and a milk frother. The DC motor holds torque at low speed, which suits whipping.

Twelve steps are enough to find a steady pace. Start at the first step and move up one at a time as the cream thickens, stopping at soft peaks. The frother head is handy for cold foam on coffee, while the whisk handles the cream.

It is the lowest in price tier among the twelve-step sticks. Rinse the whisk straight after use, check the joint for dried cream and store it dry. A solid choice for occasional bakers who want honest numbers and a gentle start.
products.bestFor: Occasional bakers who want stated rated power and a whisk.
pros: States both rated and peak power
DC motor holds torque at low speed
cons: Smaller kit than the five-piece sets

buyingCriteria.explanation: A wide wire cage traps more air than a narrow one. The Cuisinart chef's whisk and the Bonsenkitchen egg whisk are the heads that make cream, while the supplied blade turns it to butter. Check that the kit includes a whisk, since the Martha Stewart listing does not describe one.

Whipping is a slow job. The Bonsenkitchen offers twenty speeds, the Cuisinart a variable sweep and the Braun two. A stick that starts fast splashes cream and over-whips it. Pick a stick that lets you hold a moderate pace.
A tall, narrow vessel keeps the whisk submerged. The Martha Stewart one litre beaker leaves room for expansion, and the Braun beaker suits a single cup. A wide bowl lets the cream spread thin.
Cream needs little torque. A rated 350W to 400W is enough, as on the Braun and MegaWise. Spend on control rather than headline numbers.

Cream goes from soft peaks to grainy butter in under half a minute at speed. Stop when the cream holds a soft trail. A fast stick turns that margin into seconds. If you plan to pipe the cream, finish with a hand whisk for a few strokes, which gives you full control over stiffness.

Cream fat clings to wires and plastic. Warm soapy water clears it, while cold water smears it. Detachable whisks wash faster. A whisk with many fine wires holds more fat than a simple loop, so budget a minute extra for cleaning when you choose a cage design.

howWeEvaluated.title: Whisk quality
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at the whisk heads supplied. A wire cage is the right tool. The Cuisinart and Bonsenkitchen include proper whisks. A kit that offers only a blade, or a whisk with very few wires, was marked down because it cannot trap air efficiently.

howWeEvaluated.title: Low-speed range
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared how gently each stick can run, from twenty steps on the Bonsenkitchen to two on the Braun. Owner feedback patterns on over-whipped cream shaped the weighting. Because the margin between soft peaks and butter is short, a stick that can hold a steady slow pace earned the highest marks.

howWeEvaluated.title: Vessel fit
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered beaker size and shape. A tall vessel keeps the whisk submerged. The Martha Stewart beaker leads on size. We also checked that the vessel is tall enough to keep the whisk submerged without tilting, since a shallow container forces an awkward angle.

howWeEvaluated.title: Motor expectations
howWeEvaluated.description: We read the ratings, from 350W on the Braun to 1000W headlines. Cream needs little power, so we did not reward headline numbers.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value for baking
howWeEvaluated.description: We ordered the six by relative price tier, with the MegaWise and Bonsenkitchen lowest and the KOIOS highest. A baking tool should be cheap.

maintenance.task: Wash whisk wires in warm soapy water
maintenance.why: Cream fat clings to wires. Cold water smears it, while hot soapy water lifts the film in seconds, so run the whisk in a cup of warm suds and rinse until the wires squeak.
Dried cream lodges in the connection. A soft brush clears it.
A cold vessel keeps the cream stable. A warm one makes it split. Ten minutes in the freezer for the bowl and the whisk wires gives you a margin on a warm kitchen day.
Cream splash makes controls sticky. A damp cloth keeps them moving, and a quick wipe of the cord near the plug stops greasy fingerprints from collecting there.
Damp wires grow odors. Dry them fully before storing, and hang the whisk head upside down so any water in the cage can drain away from the joint.

faq.q: Can an immersion blender whip cream?
faq.a: Yes, with a whisk head. Use chilled cream in a cold, tall vessel and a slow speed. Keep the whisk just below the surface and tilt the bowl slightly, so the wires draw in air rather than slapping the top of the cream.

faq.q: Why did my cream turn to butter?
faq.a: It was over-whipped or whipped with a blade. Use a whisk head and stop at soft peaks. Once cream starts to look grainy it is on its way to butter, and adding a spoonful of fresh liquid cream and folding gently can sometimes rescue a batch that has only just tipped over.

faq.q: Do I need a strong motor?
faq.a: No. Cream needs little torque, so a rated 350W to 400W is enough. A large motor only helps when the same stick is also asked to puree soup or crush frozen fruit, and it adds nothing to the quality of the cream.

A low to moderate speed. Fast speeds splash the cream and make it split. A steady pace for about a minute usually gives soft peaks, and the sound of the whisk deepens slightly when the cream is ready.

faq.q: Can I whip egg whites too?
faq.a: Yes, in a clean, dry vessel. Any trace of fat stops them from foaming. Wipe the bowl and whisk with a little lemon juice or vinegar first if you want to be sure, and separate the eggs carefully so no yolk slips in.

Heavy or whipping cream with a high fat content. Light cream will not hold peaks. Look for a fat content of roughly thirty percent or more on the carton, and avoid ultra-pasteurised cream that has added stabilisers if you want the cleanest flavour.
